You are a senior ML research advisor synthesizing a literature review into an actionable research strategy.

**Today's date: 2026-05-30 (UTC).**

## Research area: Target: AAAI 2026
Track: Information Retrieval and Text Mining (Main Technical Track)

Direction: Train a single decoder-only LLM (Llama-3-8B) to simultaneously produce both SPLADE-style sparse representations and dense bi-encoder representations through dual output heads, with a lightweight learned query router that adaptively weights sparse vs. dense retrieval per query. The model is trained via a 3-stage curriculum (independent head pre-training, joint fine-tuning with bidirectional self-distillation, router refinement) and evaluated on MS MARCO, BEIR, and MTEB benchmarks.

Seed Papers:
- LACONIC-8B (arXiv, Jan 2026) — proves decoder-only LLMs (Llama-3-8B) achieve dense-level effectiveness for sparse retrieval via two-phase curriculum; establishes the sparse head baseline
- Scaling Sparse and Dense Retrieval in Decoder-Only LLMs (SIGIR, 2025) — systematic comparison showing sparse outperforms dense by 10.5% on BEIR at 8B scale in decoder-only models; confirms complementarity but trains separate models
- BGE M3-Embedding (arXiv, 2024) — unifies dense+sparse+multi-vec in one encoder-only model with self-KD; proves multi-functionality works but limited to XLM-RoBERTa backbone and fixed interpolation weights
- RouterRetriever (AAAI, 2025) — learned per-query routing over expert embedding models with +2.1 NDCG@10 gain; proves routing works but routes between separate dense models only
- CSplade (IJCNLP-AACL, 2025) — documents training instabilities with ReLU sparse heads in causal LMs and proposes mitigations; critical for training stability
- Sparse and Dense Retrievers Learn Better Together (CIKM, 2025) — bidirectional self-KD between sparse and dense heads improves both in VLP models; proves the self-distillation mechanism but only for text-image retrieval

Known Gaps:
- No decoder-only LLM produces both sparse AND dense representations from a single forward pass — LACONIC and Lion-SP/DS train separate models for each modality
- No learned per-query router exists WITHIN a unified retrieval model — BGE-M3 uses fixed linear interpolation; RouterRetriever routes between separate external models
- Bidirectional self-distillation between sparse and dense heads has never been studied in decoder-only backbones — only in encoder-only (BGE-M3) and VLP (CIKM 2025) models

Theoretical Anchor: Sparse and dense representations capture complementary information — sparse captures lexical matching signals (exact term overlap, entity names) while dense captures semantic matching signals (paraphrases, conceptual similarity). Lion-SP (SIGIR 2025) showed this complementarity is especially pronounced in decoder-only models (10.5% gap on BEIR). A learned router can exploit query-level signals (specificity, entity density, ambiguity) to optimally weight these complementary representations per query, achieving near-oracle hybrid performance while avoiding the latency cost of always computing both.

Constraints:
- Compute: ≤200 H100-hours (3B model: ~60hrs for 3-stage training; 8B model: ~120hrs)

Quality Self-Checks:
- [x] Core insight: Sparse and dense retrieval are complementary in decoder-only LLMs, and a learned per-query router can exploit this complementarity within a single model.
- [x] Why not obvious: Joint training of sparse and dense heads in decoder-only models faces instability (documented by CSplade); the BGE-M3 approach doesn't directly transfer because encoder-only and decoder-only attention patterns differ fundamentally; and existing routing work operates between separate models, not within a unified architecture.
- [x] Baseline fear test: Fixed-weight interpolation (the simple baseline) cannot match learned routing because the optimal sparse-dense weight varies dramatically across query types — entity-heavy queries favor sparse while conceptual queries favor dense. The router exploits query-level features that fixed weights ignore.
- [x] Information exploited: The method exploits (1) per-query lexical vs. semantic difficulty signals via the router head, (2) complementary error patterns between sparse and dense heads via bidirectional self-distillation, and (3) shared backbone representations that transfer knowledge between modalities during joint training.

Avoid:
- Fixed-weight linear interpolation between sparse and dense scores (this is the well-explored BM25+dense hybrid baseline; the contribution must be LEARNED per-query routing)
- Separate model ensembles (the contribution requires a SINGLE backbone model with shared parameters; separate sparse and dense models with a router on top is just RouterRetriever)
- ColBERT/multi-vector retrieval as a third head (adds complexity without addressing the core sparse-vs-dense question; save for future work)
- Scaling beyond 8B parameters (diminishing returns documented by SIGIR 2025; focus on architecture and training, not scale)

## Paper analyses (15 papers)

[
  {
    "title": "PromptReps: Prompting Large Language Models to Generate Dense and Sparse Representations for Zero-Shot Document Retrieval",
    "venue": "EMNLP 2024",
    "problem_identification": "No training-free method existed to extract both dense and sparse retrieval representations from a single decoder-only LLM. Prior approaches required either expensive re-ranking (limited candidate set) or large-scale contrastive training (dense only).",
    "key_insight": "A decoder-only LLM's last-token hidden states and next-token logits already encode complementary dense semantic and sparse lexical signals—prompting alone ('represent this text in one word') can surface both without any fine-tuning.",
    "innovation_type": "new_formulation",
    "method_summary": "Prompts the LLM to compress text into a single word, then extracts the last-token hidden state as a dense embedding and the next-token prediction logits (filtered to document vocabulary, ReLU + log-saturated à la SPLADE, top-128 sparsified) as a sparse bag-of-words vector. Hybrid retrieval combines both via fixed equal-weight interpolation of min-max normalized scores. Achieves 45.88 nDCG@10 on BEIR with Llama-3-8B (50.60 with BM25 fusion), competitive with trained models like E5-PT-large, scaling consistently with model size.",
    "limitations_and_open_questions": "Uses fixed equal-weight interpolation (no learned routing), zero-shot only (no fine-tuning of representations), and sparse representations are vocabulary-constrained by the LLM's tokenizer. Does the logit-based sparse signal remain complementary after supervised training, or does it collapse toward the dense head?",
    "building_blocks": [
      "Dual dense+sparse output from single decoder-only forward pass",
      "Logit-based sparse representation extraction",
      "Last-token hidden-state pooling for dense embeddings",
      "Single-word prompting paradigm for representation compression"
    ],
    "relevance_to_seed": "Directly establishes the feasibility of producing both sparse and dense representations from a single decoder-only LLM forward pass—our proposed work replaces the prompt-based extraction with learned dual heads and adds per-query routing to supersede the fixed interpolation."
  },
  {
    "title": "Improving Text Embeddings with Large Language Models (E5-Mistral)",
    "venue": "ACL 2024",
    "problem_identification": "State-of-the-art text embeddings required complex multi-stage pre-training pipelines with billions of weakly-supervised pairs, creating high engineering cost and limited task/language diversity. No work had shown decoder-only LLMs could match this with minimal fine-tuning.",
    "key_insight": "Decoder-only LLMs have already learned such rich text representations through autoregressive pre-training that contrastive pre-training is unnecessary—synthetic data generation plus brief fine-tuning (<1k steps) suffices to achieve SOTA embeddings.",
    "innovation_type": "simplification",
    "method_summary": "Uses GPT-4 to generate 500k synthetic training triplets (query, positive, hard negative) across 93 languages via a two-step brainstorming+generation pipeline covering asymmetric and symmetric task types. Fine-tunes Mistral-7B with LoRA (rank 16, 42M params) using InfoNCE loss with temperature 0.02, last-token ([EOS]) pooling, and task instructions prepended to queries only. Training completes in ~18 hours on 32 V100s. Achieves 66.6 MTEB average (+2.4 over prior SOTA) and 56.9 BEIR nDCG@10, surpassing commercial APIs.",
    "limitations_and_open_questions": "Dense-only (no sparse representations), relies on proprietary GPT-4 for data generation, and synthetic-only training drops to 46.9 BEIR (vs 56.9 with labeled data). How well does the last-token pooling paradigm extend when a sparse head competes for the same backbone capacity?",
    "building_blocks": [
      "Last-token pooling for decoder-only dense embeddings",
      "Synthetic contrastive data generation via LLMs",
      "LoRA fine-tuning of 7B+ LLMs for retrieval",
      "Query-side instruction templating"
    ],
    "relevance_to_seed": "Established the canonical paradigm for fine-tuning decoder-only LLMs for dense retrieval using contrastive loss and last-token pooling—our dense head directly follows this template, and our training curriculum builds on their finding that autoregressive pre-training eliminates the need for contrastive pre-training."
  },
  {
    "title": "DAT: Dynamic Alpha Tuning for Hybrid Retrieval in Retrieval-Augmented Generation",
    "venue": "arXiv 2025",
    "problem_identification": "Fixed-weight interpolation between sparse (BM25) and dense retrieval is universally applied despite the optimal weight varying dramatically across queries. The authors identified 'hybrid-sensitive queries'—where BM25 and dense rank documents differently—as the failure mode of fixed weighting.",
    "key_insight": "An LLM can evaluate the quality of each retrieval method's top-1 result per query, and the ratio of these effectiveness scores provides a principled, query-adaptive interpolation weight without any training.",
    "innovation_type": "new_technique",
    "method_summary": "Retrieves top-1 documents from BM25 and dense retrieval independently, then prompts an LLM to score each on a 0-5 scale assessing factual alignment. Computes query-specific alpha via case logic: α=0.5 when both fail (scores=0), α=1.0 or 0.0 when one achieves a perfect score, otherwise α=S_dense/(S_dense+S_bm25). Final ranking uses α-weighted interpolation of normalized scores. On hybrid-sensitive queries, achieves +6-7.5% Precision@1 over fixed α=0.6 baselines on SQuAD and DRCD.",
    "limitations_and_open_questions": "Requires LLM inference per query (significant latency overhead acknowledged in appendix), only evaluated on 2 small QA datasets (~3k queries each), evaluates only top-1 document (ignores ranking quality beyond rank 1), and the case-based alpha formula is hand-crafted rather than learned. Can a lightweight trained router match this quality without LLM-at-inference cost?",
    "building_blocks": [
      "Per-query adaptive sparse-dense interpolation weights",
      "LLM-as-judge for retrieval effectiveness scoring",
      "Case-based alpha computation formula",
      "Hybrid-sensitive query identification methodology"
    ],
    "relevance_to_seed": "Validates the core hypothesis that per-query adaptive weighting substantially outperforms fixed interpolation—our learned router head internalizes this principle without requiring LLM inference at query time, achieving the same adaptivity at zero additional latency cost."

    "title": "Learning Effective Representations for Retrieval Using Self-Distillation with Adaptive Relevance Margins",
    "venue": "ICTIR 2025",
    "problem_identification": "Training bi-encoder retrievers requires either expensive cross-encoder teachers (TAS-B, ColBERT-distill) or carefully tuned margin hyperparameters (MarginMSE). No parameter-free alternative existed that could exploit the encoder's own pre-trained knowledge as supervision.",
    "key_insight": "The encoder's pre-trained masked language modeling capabilities already encode text similarity—using cosine similarity between positive and negative document embeddings as an adaptive margin target provides a parameter-free self-distillation signal that implicitly mines hard negatives.",
    "innovation_type": "simplification",
    "method_summary": "Replaces the static margin ε in triplet loss with an adaptive target: margin = (1+cos(d⁺,d⁻))/2, computed from the training encoder's own document embeddings. When d⁺ and d⁻ are similar (hard negatives), the target approaches 1.0, creating larger gradients—achieving implicit hard negative mining without sampling. The distributed variant averages targets across batch negatives: l_ij = φ(q,d⁺)-φ(q,d⁻_j)-(1+φ(d⁺,d⁻_j))/2. Matches TAS-B effectiveness using only 13.5% of training data with 3-15x speedup. Tested on RoBERTa, MPNet, and distilBERT (66-124M params).",
    "limitations_and_open_questions": "BEIR zero-shot performance drops notably (0.341 vs TAS-B's 0.430 nDCG@10), susceptible to overfitting without early stopping, and only validated on BERT-scale encoders. Does the self-distillation signal remain useful in decoder-only architectures where the pre-trained similarity signal comes from autoregressive rather than masked LM objectives?",

      "Parameter-free adaptive margin from encoder's own embeddings",
      "Implicit hard negative mining via document similarity scaling",
      "Distributed targets across batch negatives",
      "Self-distillation without external teacher models"
    ],
    "relevance_to_seed": "The core self-distillation principle—using one representation's similarity signal as training target for another—directly informs our bidirectional self-distillation between sparse and dense heads, though we must adapt it from single-head self-supervision to cross-head knowledge transfer in a decoder-only backbone."
  },
  {
    "title": "Generative Representational Instruction Tuning (GritLM)",
    "venue": "ICLR 2025 (Oral)",
    "problem_identification": "Embedding models and generative LLMs were trained separately, requiring two models in RAG pipelines and doubling compute/memory. No prior work showed a single decoder-only model could achieve SOTA on both tasks simultaneously without degradation.",
    "key_insight": "Embedding and generation are not competing objectives—a single LLM can switch between bidirectional attention (for embeddings via mean pooling) and causal attention (for generation) using instruction-based task routing, with zero performance loss on either task.",
    "innovation_type": "combination",
    "method_summary": "GritLM finetunes a pretrained LLM (Mistral-7B or 8x7B) with a combined loss: contrastive loss with in-batch negatives for embedding (using bidirectional attention + mean pooling) and next-token prediction loss for generation (using causal attention). A special <|embed|> token triggers embedding mode. Training uses E5S embedding data and Tülu-2 generative data, with representation loss weighted higher since generative capability is already pretrained. Crucially, in RAG, embeddings from the retrieval pass are reused for generation, saving one full forward pass and yielding >60% speedup.",
    "limitations_and_open_questions": "Evaluation limited to 512-token sequences due to MTEB constraints; unclear how bidirectional attention finetuning affects long-context generative performance. Does not explore sparse retrieval heads—only dense embeddings paired with generation.",
    "building_blocks": [
      "Instruction-based task switching in decoder-only LLMs",
      "Bidirectional attention for embedding in causally-pretrained models",
      "Joint contrastive + generative loss training",
      "Embedding reuse across retrieval and generation passes"
    ],
    "relevance_to_seed": "Directly validates that a single decoder-only LLM can support multiple output modalities (embedding + generation) via task-specific attention patterns—architectural precedent for our dual sparse/dense heads with learned routing."
  },
  {
    "title": "Mistral-SPLADE: LLMs for Better Learned Sparse Retrieval",
    "venue": "arXiv 2024",
    "problem_identification": "All prior SPLADE variants used encoder-only (BERT-class) backbones with MLM heads, limiting term expansion quality to the encoder's pretraining knowledge. No work had successfully deployed SPLADE on a decoder-only LLM despite their vastly richer pretraining.",
    "key_insight": "Decoder-only LLMs' superior pretraining enables dramatically better semantic keyword expansion for sparse retrieval, but causal masking must be circumvented via Echo embeddings (duplicating input so the second copy's tokens see full bidirectional context).",
    "innovation_type": "cross_domain",
    "method_summary": "Echo-Mistral-SPLADE feeds each input twice (concatenated), extracting SPLADE representations only from the second occurrence where all tokens have full context via causal attention over the first copy. It uses QLoRA finetuning (avoiding expensive weight-tying reinitialization), InfoNCE contrastive loss with in-batch negatives (batch size 512), and FLOPS regularization with quadratic scheduling to control sparsity. Trained on 15.5M sentence-transformer pairs rather than MS MARCO alone, eliminating the need for hard negative mining while achieving SOTA on BEIR with 5.8% relative nDCG@10 gain over prior SPLADE variants.",
    "limitations_and_open_questions": "Echo embedding doubles sequence length, increasing compute and limiting max document length. Only sparse retrieval is explored—no dense head or hybrid within the same model. No MS MARCO in-domain evaluation reported, focusing solely on zero-shot BEIR transfer.",
    "building_blocks": [
      "Echo embedding technique for decoder-only sparse retrieval",
      "QLoRA for efficient SPLADE finetuning on LLMs",
      "FLOPS regularization with quadratic scheduling",
      "Sentence-transformer data as universal training source for sparse models"
    ],
    "relevance_to_seed": "Validates the sparse head component of our architecture on decoder-only LLMs and provides the Echo embedding workaround for causal masking, directly informing our SPLADE-style sparse output head design on Llama-3-8B."
  },
  {
    "title": "MoR: Better Handling Diverse Queries with a Mixture of Sparse, Dense, and Human Retrievers",
    "venue": "EMNLP 2025",
    "problem_identification": "RAG systems use a single fixed retriever, but different query types benefit from different retrieval modalities (lexical vs. semantic). Prior hybrid approaches used fixed interpolation weights, ignoring query-level variation in retriever effectiveness.",
    "key_insight": "Per-query retriever weighting can be computed zero-shot using unsupervised pre-retrieval signals (query-corpus embedding alignment via K-means centroids) and post-retrieval signals (Moran spatial autocorrelation of retrieved documents), without any labeled relevance data.",
    "innovation_type": "new_technique",
    "method_summary": "MoR computes per-query weights for each retriever using three signals: (1) pre-retrieval corpus familiarity (distance from query embedding to K-means cluster centroids in each retriever's space), (2) post-retrieval Moran coefficient (spatial correlation among top-20 retrieved documents), and (3) post-retrieval document-corpus alignment. Weights are combined as f_post = 0.1·V_pre + 0.3·I_Moran + 0.6·V_post with fixed coefficients. Coverage is expanded 4× via multi-granularity decomposition (questions/sub-questions × documents/propositions). Score normalization to [0,1] handles heterogeneous retriever scales. Despite 0.8B total parameters, it beats 7B single-retriever models by +3.9%.",
    "limitations_and_open_questions": "Mixture coefficients (0.1/0.3/0.6) are fixed hyperparameters, not learned—a learned version could further improve. Operates over separate external retrievers rather than within a unified model. Human retriever integration is simulated, not validated with real expert retrieval.",
    "building_blocks": [
      "Unsupervised pre/post-retrieval quality signals for routing",
      "Moran coefficient as retriever confidence estimator",
      "Multi-granularity query/document decomposition for retriever ensembles",
      "Score normalization for heterogeneous retriever fusion"
    ],
    "relevance_to_seed": "Provides strong empirical evidence that per-query adaptive weighting of sparse vs. dense retrieval outperforms fixed interpolation—directly motivating our learned router, which could replace MoR's fixed coefficients with a trained routing head inside a unified model."
  },
  {
    "title": "Repurposing Language Models into Embedding Models: Finding the Compute-Optimal Recipe",
    "venue": "NeurIPS 2024",
    "problem_identification": "Practitioners converting decoder-only LLMs into embedding models lacked principled guidance on model size, data quantity, and finetuning method selection under fixed compute budgets. Prior scaling laws (Chinchilla) covered pretraining but not contrastive finetuning.",
    "key_insight": "Full finetuning and LoRA have a compute-budget crossover point (~9.06×10¹⁶ FLOP): full finetuning wins below it, LoRA wins above it—and the optimal model size is often counter-intuitively NOT the largest available.",
    "innovation_type": "scaling",
    "method_summary": "The authors extend Chinchilla-style scaling laws to contrastive finetuning by introducing a trainable-parameter-fraction term S into the loss prediction formula: L(S,N,D) incorporates how partial parameter updates (LoRA, block freezing) interact with model size N and data D. Key practical findings: bias-only tuning is always suboptimal; LoRA rank 32–128 is robust; block freezing offers memory savings at large budgets; and the crossover between full FT and LoRA occurs at ~9×10¹⁶ FLOP.",

Single runs per configuration (no error bars). Only contrastive loss studied; unclear if findings hold for joint contrastive + sparse (SPLADE) objectives.",

      "Compute-optimal scaling laws for contrastive finetuning",
      "IsoFLOP analysis for embedding model design",
      "LoRA vs full FT crossover budget threshold",
      "Algorithm for budget-to-configuration mapping"
    ],
    "relevance_to_seed": "Directly informs our 200 H100-hour training budget decisions: at Llama-3-8B scale, the crossover analysis suggests whether LoRA or full finetuning is optimal for each training stage, and the scaling law framework could guide data quantity choices for our 3-stage curriculum."
  },
  {
    "title": "NV-Embed: Improved Techniques for Training LLMs as Generalist Embedding Models",
    "venue": "ICLR 2025 (Spotlight)",
    "problem_identification": "Decoder-only LLMs used as embedding backbones suffer from (1) pooling that either dilutes information (mean) or has recency bias (EOS-token), (2) causal attention that artificially restricts information flow when full input is available, and (3) task conflicts when mixing retrieval (needs in-batch negatives) with non-retrieval tasks (where in-batch negatives cause label collisions). Identified through systematic ablation of existing decoder-only embedding pipelines.",
    "key_insight": "Removing the causal attention mask during contrastive training (not pretraining) unlocks bidirectional context for embedding tasks, and a latent attention layer using trainable prototype vectors acts as a learned dictionary that extracts task-relevant features before pooling — together enabling a decoder-only LLM to outperform purpose-built embedding models.",

    "method_summary": "Inserts a cross-attention layer with 512 trainable latent vectors on top of Mistral-7B's final hidden states, where token representations attend to these prototypes before mean-pooling through an MLP. Uses a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 trains on 15+ retrieval datasets with in-batch + hard negatives; Stage 2 blends retrieval data with classification/clustering/STS tasks, disabling in-batch negatives for non-retrieval tasks to avoid label collisions. Hard negatives mined via E5-Mistral with a 95% positive-score threshold.",

      "Bidirectional attention removal for decoder-only embeddings",
      "Two-stage retrieval-first contrastive instruction-tuning",
      "Task-aware in-batch negative toggling",
      "Positive-aware hard negative mining"

    "relevance_to_seed": "Directly applicable to the dense head design: latent attention pooling and bidirectional attention removal should be adopted for the dense embedding head, and the two-stage curriculum validates the proposed multi-stage training approach."

    "title": "Scaling Laws for Dense Retrieval",
    "venue": "SIGIR 2024 (Best Paper Award)",

    "key_insight": "Contrastive entropy — the contrastive log-likelihood of retrieving a relevant document — serves as a smooth, continuous proxy for ranking metrics, enabling power-law fitting; crucially, because retrieval requires encoding entire corpora, inference cost (not training cost) dominates the budget, inverting the 'bigger is better' wisdom from language modeling.",

Derives a joint model-data scaling law and a lifecycle cost model incorporating annotation, training, and inference costs. Discovers that the model-size exponent α≈0.53 is consistent across datasets, and identifies an emergent ability threshold at CE≈0.25 where ranking performance sharply improves.",

LLM-generated annotations surpassing human labels at 500k+ scale needs validation across more domains.",

      "Inference-cost-aware budget allocation framework",

    "relevance_to_seed": "Directly informs compute budget allocation for the 3B/8B training — the inference-cost dominance finding suggests favoring the 3B model with more data over the 8B model, and the scaling exponents enable principled resource planning within the 200 H100-hour budget."

    "title": "SPLARE: Learning Retrieval Models with Sparse Autoencoders",
    "venue": "arXiv 2026 (submitted to ICLR 2026)",
    "problem_identification": "SPLADE-style learned sparse retrieval projects onto vocabulary space, inheriting three fundamental limitations: (1) vocabulary tokens are designed for tokenization, not semantic representation, causing redundancy (e.g., 'Indian'/'indian' as separate dimensions); (2) subword tokenizers are biased toward high-resource languages, crippling multilingual transfer; (3) dimensionality is fixed by vocabulary size.     "key_insight": "Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on LLM residual streams for mechanistic interpretability already produce sparse, monosemantic, language-agnostic features — making them a natural drop-in replacement for vocabulary projection in sparse retrieval, with the bonus that only intermediate-layer computation is needed (not full forward pass).",

## Research area: Target: AAAI 2026
Track: Information Retrieval and Text Mining (Main Technical Track)

Direction: Train a single decoder-only LLM (Llama-3-8B) to simultaneously produce both SPLADE-style sparse representations and dense bi-encoder representations through dual output heads, with a lightweight learned query router that adaptively weights sparse vs. dense retrieval per query. The model is trained via a 3-stage curriculum (independent head pre-training, joint fine-tuning with bidirectional self-distillation, router refinement) and evaluated on MS MARCO, BEIR, and MTEB benchmarks.

Seed Papers:
- LACONIC-8B (arXiv, Jan 2026) — proves decoder-only LLMs (Llama-3-8B) achieve dense-level effectiveness for sparse retrieval via two-phase curriculum; establishes the sparse head baseline
- Scaling Sparse and Dense Retrieval in Decoder-Only LLMs (SIGIR, 2025) — systematic comparison showing sparse outperforms dense by 10.5% on BEIR at 8B scale in decoder-only models; confirms complementarity but trains separate models
- BGE M3-Embedding (arXiv, 2024) — unifies dense+sparse+multi-vec in one encoder-only model with self-KD; proves multi-functionality works but limited to XLM-RoBERTa backbone and fixed interpolation weights
- RouterRetriever (AAAI, 2025) — learned per-query routing over expert embedding models with +2.1 NDCG@10 gain; proves routing works but routes between separate dense models only
- CSplade (IJCNLP-AACL, 2025) — documents training instabilities with ReLU sparse heads in causal LMs and proposes mitigations; critical for training stability
- Sparse and Dense Retrievers Learn Better Together (CIKM, 2025) — bidirectional self-KD between sparse and dense heads improves both in VLP models; proves the self-distillation mechanism but only for text-image retrieval

Known Gaps:
- No decoder-only LLM produces both sparse AND dense representations from a single forward pass — LACONIC and Lion-SP/DS train separate models for each modality
- No learned per-query router exists WITHIN a unified retrieval model — BGE-M3 uses fixed linear interpolation; RouterRetriever routes between separate external models
- Bidirectional self-distillation between sparse and dense heads has never been studied in decoder-only backbones — only in encoder-only (BGE-M3) and VLP (CIKM 2025) models

Theoretical Anchor: Sparse and dense representations capture complementary information — sparse captures lexical matching signals (exact term overlap, entity names) while dense captures semantic matching signals (paraphrases, conceptual similarity). Lion-SP (SIGIR 2025) showed this complementarity is especially pronounced in decoder-only models (10.5% gap on BEIR). A learned router can exploit query-level signals (specificity, entity density, ambiguity) to optimally weight these complementary representations per query, achieving near-oracle hybrid performance while avoiding the latency cost of always computing both.

Constraints:
- Compute: ≤200 H100-hours (3B model: ~60hrs for 3-stage training; 8B model: ~120hrs)

Quality Self-Checks:
- [x] Core insight: Sparse and dense retrieval are complementary in decoder-only LLMs, and a learned per-query router can exploit this complementarity within a single model.
- [x] Why not obvious: Joint training of sparse and dense heads in decoder-only models faces instability (documented by CSplade); the BGE-M3 approach doesn't directly transfer because encoder-only and decoder-only attention patterns differ fundamentally; and existing routing work operates between separate models, not within a unified architecture.
- [x] Baseline fear test: Fixed-weight interpolation (the simple baseline) cannot match learned routing because the optimal sparse-dense weight varies dramatically across query types — entity-heavy queries favor sparse while conceptual queries favor dense. The router exploits query-level features that fixed weights ignore.
- [x] Information exploited: The method exploits (1) per-query lexical vs. semantic difficulty signals via the router head, (2) complementary error patterns between sparse and dense heads via bidirectional self-distillation, and (3) shared backbone representations that transfer knowledge between modalities during joint training.

Avoid:
- Fixed-weight linear interpolation between sparse and dense scores (this is the well-explored BM25+dense hybrid baseline; the contribution must be LEARNED per-query routing)
- Separate model ensembles (the contribution requires a SINGLE backbone model with shared parameters; separate sparse and dense models with a router on top is just RouterRetriever)
- ColBERT/multi-vector retrieval as a third head (adds complexity without addressing the core sparse-vs-dense question; save for future work)
- Scaling beyond 8B parameters (diminishing returns documented by SIGIR 2025; focus on architecture and training, not scale)

1. Unification/Multi-task in single model - BGE-M3, GritLM, PromptReps all unify multiple capabilities

3. Self-distillation without external teachers - ICTIR 2025 adaptive margins, BGE-M3's self-KD
4. Cross-domain transfer of techniques - SPLARE (SAEs from interpretability to IR), Mistral-SPLADE (decoder-only for sparse)

6. Per-query adaptation - DAT, MoR, RouterRetriever

- Ablation studies that isolate each component's contribution
- Strong baselines (not strawmen)
- Compute efficiency / practical deployment considerations
- Zero-shot transfer

I'm also noticing scaling laws for sparse retrieval haven't been established, and there's no direct comparison between SAE-based and vocabulary-based sparse approaches. The untried combinations that stand out are combining dual heads with a learned router in one decoder-only model, using SAE sparse with dense heads together, applying anchor enrichment bidirectionally across both heads, and figuring out compute-optimal scaling when training joint sparse and dense objectives.

The common pitfalls I need to avoid are ReLU instability in causal language models, how causal attention itself limits representation quality, relying on fixed interpolation as a baseline, skipping zero-shot BEIR evaluation, and overstating novelty when it's really just combining existing pieces. The field is clearly moving toward unified models with decoder-only architectures, learned routing, and efficiency gains, so I should focus on what's architecturally novel rather than just integrating known techniques.

For this work, I need to emphasize the training curriculum, run strong ablations, and make sure the design is compute-aware.
